summary:
NasaRoads is a web application we developed to help drivers compare routes when poor road conditions or rain make travel difficult. Its goal is to show how much extra time a route would take if it avoids more of the affected road segments.

The demo starts with an interactive globe. Users select Bolivia, Santa Cruz Department, Santa Cruz de la Sierra. As they zoom into the city, the map displays its streets and lets them choose a starting point and a destination. In dry conditions, the app compares the estimated fastest route with an alternative that prioritizes better pavement. In rainy conditions, it combines NASA POWER precipitation data with the OpenStreetMap road network.
details:
NasaRoads is a web application that lets users compare routes based on pavement conditions and past flooding reports in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, Bolivia. The demo starts with an interactive globe where users select Bolivia, the Santa Cruz department, and the city of Santa Cruz de la Sierra. On the street map, they choose a starting point and a destination to calculate two routes.

In Dry Route mode, the app compares the estimated fastest route with an alternative that prioritizes streets with better pavement based on the data available in OpenStreetMap. Icons for potholes, cracks, and road depressions are labeled as simulated examples. In Rainy Route mode, the app combines historical precipitation data from NASA POWER with the road network and a local report of water accumulation. In the October 1, 2025 scenario, the detour to Clínica CIES La Ramada avoids 333 meters of the reported area and adds 1.1 minutes to the estimated travel time.

What makes the project creative is that users can see why the route changes. They can move the pins, explore alerts along each route, and see on the same map which road segments are affected and how much extra time the detour would take. Our goal is to help drivers consider road conditions when planning a trip.

We built the app with Python and Streamlit, used Leaflet and D3.js for the maps, and used NetworkX to calculate the routes. The data comes from NASA POWER Daily, OpenStreetMap, and a local report from El Deber. The explorer also offers an optional terrain layer from NASA GIBS. The demo runs in a web browser and requires no dedicated sensors.

When calculating routes, we considered permitted directions of travel, recorded or estimated speeds, and the data available for each road segment. The rain scenario is historical. The app distinguishes road segments covered by the report from those with no available information. Water depth is unknown.
